meaningMnemonic: What's something useful you can get out of a tree? A book ! Just cut that book right out of the tree trunk. If you think about it, every tree contains unlimited book potential. It's just a shame they have to be cut down to make the books…

This radical looks like a fancy composite bow people would use to shoot at targets and definitely not any normal living animals. See how the middle part is being pulled back? Imagine holding this bow and firing it at a target shaped like a giant alligator-crab monster.
This is the radical for child . Aww, see how they're wearing a cap and have their little arms stretched out? You can almost hear them saying "pick me up!" A very child-like child.

This is the cow radical. It kind of looks like the long face of a cow, right? You can think of that top horizontal line as its horns. Seeing it yet? It's got a little tuft of hair on its head, and some kind of accessory on the horn to your left, so this is a very stylish cow. (Did you know both male and female cows can have horns? I didn't either, but it's true. So please don't write in telling us we can't call this thing a cow — we don't want any beef.)

At first this looks like a cross in the ground, but it's actually something growing in the dirt . It's a little sprout, already rocking three leaves. And it's all thanks to that dirt! When you see this radical, think about how amazing it is that things just, like, grow in the dirt.
Remember the big guy who helped you with that big radical? Now you've got his big DOG ! You know it's a dog because he's lying down, legs all spread out, with his favorite bone right beside his head.

This is the top half of a moon peeking out as it begins to rise. When does that happen? In the evening ! Don't confuse this with the moon radical 月 . 夕 is for the evening, when the moon's still low enough to be partly covered (by a mountain, for example).

See the iris in the middle of the eyeball? Remember that there are no round things in kanji, so square things take their place. That makes this a pretty realistic, square eye . You just have to squint with your real eyes a bit.

This is the radical for fire . It's got three little flames on top and even a couple logs underneath. But if it helps you can also focus on the person radical here. See it? It's got things coming off of it... What are those thi— OH MY GOD IT'S FIRE!!! Help, help! Put the fire out! Wait, it's fine… It's just the fire radical.

If you use your imagination, this radical actually looks like the number "5." You just have to remove the vertical line in the bottom left, plus a few extra ends that stick out here and there. Once you do that, you have an easy way to remember that this radical means five .
See the flag in this radical? There's a pole with a flag on the end of it, blowing in the wind. Basically, this radical looks just like a flag.
These three streaks look like the flowing locks of someone's hair . Pretty easy to see and remember that this is the hair radical, right?

This is the hand radical. If you look at the palm of your right hand, the lines in it probably kinda look like the lines in 手 . Sure it's not a perfect match, and everyone's got different hands, but basically this radical looks like the lines in your hand. You could also think of the horizontal lines in 手 as fingers. That would make for a pretty alien-looking hand, but still a hand… of sorts…

This is the outline of a head . A really square head, admittedly, but try to imagine it facing to the right. The left side is the back of the head, and the barb-like part on the right shows the curve of the chin. See the head?

Remember the guy from the big radical? This is him again, but this time he's so big his head is touching heaven . He's looking up and has his arms stretched open toward heaven, and his big hair is poking into those heavenly clouds.

This is the king radical. Picture this king sitting on his solid, squarish throne. The top stroke is the high back of the throne. The cross in the middle is his body, with his arms spread out on the arm rests. The bottom stroke is the ground. See him sitting there now, looking all dignified. Talk about a kingly king.
There's a leaf on top and a stem going down out of it, making this the leaf radical. It's a pretty wide and flat leaf, so if it helps you can imagine it as a lily pad leaf.
This radical already looks like a pair of legs . There's even feet on these legs. That's how you know these are legs and not fins (or something else).

This is a stick going through the middle of a mouth. What kind of mouth? Mouth of a cylinder, mouth of a box, a human mouth — whatever kind you want to imagine, as long as the stick is going through the middle of it, since this is the radical for "middle."

This is the moon radical. See how it looks like a crescent moon with a couple of little clouds floating by? Try not to mix this up with the evening radical 夕 — you can see the whole crescent moon this time, so obviously this should be the radical for moon!

This radical looks like a narwhal . See the tail at the bottom, and the majestic narwhal horn poking out at the top? It also looks like the katakana character ナ (na), so you can remember it that way too. Na-na-na-narwhal! Just be careful not to confuse this with the treasure radical ( メ ). The sideways line for that one is at more of a downward angle, like an "X." But the sideways line for narwhal is horizontal ( ナ ).

This is a little triangle that's almost completely closed off. When you want to be alone, you hide in a place where you can be in private . That's why this is the private radical. You're closing yourself off to the rest of the world, with just a little peephole.

In Japan rice paddies are made up of square fields with irrigation lines going between them. See the four rice paddies with water flowing between and around them? That's why this radical is rice paddy .

You see two fins around a barb, but when you look closer, you realize those fins are actually two tiny fish. Think how small these fins (and fish) would have to be to look so much smaller than an already small barb. Talk about small fry… Yeah, that's why this is the radical for small .
This looks like someone in a standing position with legs planted firmly on the ground, spreading their arms out in a T-pose to maintain balance. So that makes this the radical for stand .

There's a stick and a giant toe stuck in the ground. Imagine walking along and seeing these things in your path. What would you do? Most likely come to a complete stop . You know, because of the toe. I guess a normal stop sign wasn't good enough, so they also put up this big toe to really get people to stop.
Imagine viewing this one from above — looks like a couple of streets, right? Maybe a three-way intersection at the top there? Well, that's why this is the radical for street .

This is the sword radical. The ノ part is the curvy sword, while the rest is a samurai bowing deeply, like 90 degrees, as he holds that sword — probably before a sword fight. By the way, don't confuse this with the power radical ( 力 ). See the difference? In the sword radical ( 刀 ), the ノ doesn't pierce through the bowing samurai. (Lucky for him.)

You have a slide supported by a big cross, which makes it so strong it can hold a lot of people at once. How many? A THOUSAND ! Imagine a thousand people going down this slide. You can hear a voice trying to count them as they go: "ONE! TWO! THREE HUNDRED! FIVE HUNDRED!" and so on. Finally the last person slides down and the voice calls out: "A THOUSAND!" You think it's over, but just as that group finishes, in come another thousand…
This radical is treasure because "X marks the spot," as they say. Doesn't it look like the X on a pirate treasure map? You want to go find that treasure now, right?!

This is the radical for water . It's the water radical because it kind of looks like water coming out of a faucet and splashing everywhere. See how it flows off in different directions too? Very water-like! As water-like as a radical can be, anyway…

Add a drop of the sun to something and it will turn it white . The sun is really strong, so even a single drop will burn anything white. Why do you think so many beaches are white? Even the drops of sunblock you use to stop the sun's rays is white. So when you think of sun drops, think white.

This looks like a stool with a lid on it, but it's actually a desk for writing . Do you see it? You can even see the pen sticking up in the middle. Think of all the beautiful writing that's been produced here. Letters, novels, essays — any kind of writing you can think of.

The king has a big drop of liquid in his hand... but then he bounces it! The drop was really a ball . Hints This kanji looks just like a king bouncing a ball , no? If not, imagine the kanji itself bouncing the drop (the ball ) over and over again. Kanji are surprisingly playful like that.
readingMnemonic: When he's done playing with it, the king gives his ball to Tama ra ( たま ), the resident ball girl, for safekeeping. Hints Try to remember Tamara the ball girl. She'll come up anytime the reading for a kanji is たま , and usually she'll be involved with some kind of ball or round object. That's her job, after all.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for book first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means book as well. Take note that the second, third, and fourth meanings of this kanji are origin , real , and main . You can figure this out by thinking about how books mainly have their origins in real life. Hints Make sure you know those radicals, yo! And good luck with all the meanings (sorry sorry sorry).
readingMnemonic: Book s are one of the best ways to hone ( ほん ) your intellect, you know? Hints Just think about books and how you use them to hone your skills. Or read a book about honing things. Like swords.

meaningMnemonic: The child radical and the child kanji are exactly the same. Hints So, if you know your radicals, you know your kanji as well! This won't last forever (where radicals are exactly the same as the kanji) so enjoy it while the kanji are still small and simple!
readingMnemonic: The main reading here is し , so to remember it we'll use this mnemonic: There is a child standing in front of you. You look closely at the child but something seems wrong. You rub your eyes and when you open them again, there is a shee p ( し ) in front of you. A sheep?! You yelp, blink again, and it's back to being a child. Are… are all children really just sheep? Hints The child (sheep) runs away and you chase after it. Every time it's about to turn a corner it looks like a sheep again, but whenever you yell and point, it changes back into a child. You're the only one who can see this sheep child!

meaningMnemonic: What's something with nine sides? Just add a drop and you'll have something that's almost a circle . Hints It's not quite a circle though. You just need to add a drop of liquid to the edges to smooth it out to become a full circle.
readingMnemonic: Do you know about the adorable cat Maru? If not, you should check it out . May seem like a distraction, but if you come back knowing the reading for this kanji, then it's totally worthwhile. When you think about a circle, think about Maru all rolled up in a little circle, being super adorable. Don't tell me it doesn't melt your heart just thinking about it. Alternatively, you could also look at this kanji and think of Maru inside of a box, with his little tail sticking out of it. Whatever works best for you, just get yourself to "Maru." Hints Obviously if you "don't know this reading" well enough, you should watch some more Maru videos. I'll understand... just make sure you come back someday, okay?

meaningMnemonic: There is a line on the ground so you stop , making a giant sign pop up that says CORRECT ! You obeyed the rules of the road and did the correct thing. Good on you. Hints Imagine walking, staring at the ground until you come across a line that you're supposed to stop at. If you stop, the big "correct" sign appears, chiming a happy tune.
readingMnemonic: You did the correct thing, so here's your reward: a sa ber ( せい ) from the Shou gun ( しょう ) himself! Hints Perhaps a slightly unorthodox weapon for a ruler of medieval Japan, but you won't complain about a saber from the Shogun himself!

meaningMnemonic: The dirt radical and the dirt kanji are the same! Hints As long as you know the radical dirt, you know the kanji dirt.
readingMnemonic: Who spends a lot of time in dirt ? Do gs ( ど ) do! Dogs dig in dirt, they roll in dirt, sometimes they try to eat dirt (which isn't so great). Hints Dogs and dirt just go together!

meaningMnemonic: The dog radical and dog kanji are exactly the same! Hints Soon there will be very few kanji/radical-same combos ... so enjoy it while you can.
readingMnemonic: Every dog likes to ea t noo dles ( いぬ ). Like that movie where the dogs share a noodle and end up kissing, right? So when you see 犬 , just imagine how those two eat noodles. Hints P.S. Don't actually let your dog eat noodles, at least not with marinara sauce. Disney didn't show you how that Lady and Tramp date probably ended — unromantically, with indigestion.

meaningMnemonic: The evening radical and the evening kanji are the same. If you know the radical you know the meaning of the kanji. Hints Do what you're meant to do. Study those radicals!
readingMnemonic: The evening is when all the you ths ( ゆう ) come outside to play. Hints Young people love staying up the entire evening doing youth-people things, and it's really obnoxious for us curmudgeonly folk. Note: All the ゆう readings will use the word "youths" as a keyword for the mnemonic, so bear that in mind for any future ゆう reading you'll encounter.

meaningMnemonic: There are two mountains in front of you... and probably a bunch more around you too. You are in a pass, and don't know how to get out. You are frantically looking for the exit before you freeze to death. The most important thing is to find the exit from this mountain range - your life depends on it. Hints In your imagination, really feel like your life depends on getting out. The important part is the feeling of "needing to get out of the mountain pass." If you have this feeling, you'll be more likely to remember that this kanji means exit, because that's what you want to do when you see this kanji.
readingMnemonic: As you're trying to exit this mountain range, you suddenly realize that someone is actually hunting you. What? Make sure to feel that sudden realization. It's crazy. Then, you find the exit and run towards it. Sadly, the hunter is waiting there, and he shoots you ( しゅつ ) through the leg, knocking you down. Hints Focus on the surprise of realizing you're being hunted while trying to find the exit to the mountain range, then focus on the next part, where you get shot. View it in your head as the hunter shooting you. Powww!

meaningMnemonic: The eye radical and eye kanji are the same as each other, so now you know them both. Hints Well... you'll know them both as long as you studied your radicals, young grasshopper. If you didn't, then you're just a young grasshopper who needs to study their radicals.
readingMnemonic: Your eyes are important to you, right? Sadly, one of your eyes is missing right now, because a sheep grabbed it and pulled it out, and is now running away from you, yelling his sheep call.... " Mehhhhhh ( め )!" Hints Of course, feel the pain of your eye being gone... and struggle to get it back. You eventually give up because the sheep is too fast, but then you come up with an idea. What if I call out back to the sheep in its own language? Go ahead and cover one eye and start making "MEHHH" noises to see if you can get the sheep to come back to you and give you your eye. It's up to you whether it works or not, but be sure to feel frustrated by its reaction, or happy by it. Either one works.

meaningMnemonic: The fire radical and the fire kanji are the same as each other. Hints If you know the radicals then this one is EZPZ.
readingMnemonic: Whenever we need to remember か , we use the word car . For this kanji, when we think fire , we ought to think of something on fire. What's on fire? It's obviously your very own car ( か )! Oh Goddd NOOO! Hints Oh no... Oh no!! If you don't have a car , imagine what it'd feel like if your car just exploded and burned down. If you do have a car, imagine your own car in this situation. It should be a terrible feeling, if you imagine it well enough. So, when you think fire , remember the fear you had when your car was given to the flames. Now you have to walk everywhere, sad :(

meaningMnemonic: The five radical and the five kanji are the same. Hints Know your radicals, friend-o.
readingMnemonic: Five is the number of buildings Go dzilla ( ご ) will knock down. Oh, look! There he goes now. Hints One, two, three, four, five—GODZILLA IS HERE GO GO, RUN!

meaningMnemonic: Imagine contorting yourself in such a way that your mouth now has your legs inside it. You've bent your body in all the wrong ways to achieve this. In fact, if you look at yourself, you look like a square now... You're just a person with four sides. Hints If you can see this kanji as a kind of square, you should be able to remember it means "four" as well, since squares always have four sides.
readingMnemonic: Now that you have four sides, you look like a four-sided animal: the shee p ( し ). Look at yourself in the mirror and see an adorable four-sided sheep looking back at you. Imagine yourself with perfectly square wool. (You can only see four sides because mirrors aren't 3D. So you're a flat, cartoonish sheep.) Hints What's better than a four-sided sheep?

meaningMnemonic: The hand radical and the hand kanji are identical in looks and meaning! That should make things easy! Hints Make sure you're studying your radicals. It won't be forever that radicals and kanji overlap so nicely like this!
readingMnemonic: To remember the reading て we will use the word "television." You have great hands. Go ahead and look at them. OH MY GOD. You have little te levisions ( て ) on your hands. They are playing the dumbest show you can think of, too, both hands at the same time. Hints You try to shake your hands off, but it's no good. The televisions are stuck, and the volume won't go down. You have no idea how you got these televisions on your hands. All you know is that you want them off right this instant.

meaningMnemonic: The radical heaven is the same as the kanji heaven , making this an easy kanji to memorize. Hints If you know your radicals well (and you should!) you know the meaning of this kanji well, as well!
readingMnemonic: Heaven ... nowadays, people aren't all that good. Things have gotten bad. That's why the acceptance rate to get into heaven is only ten ( てん ) percent! Hints Imagine yourself in line to get into heaven. You're super worried, because you're not sure if you'll get in. You heard there was a one in ten chance... those aren't good odds. Feel nervous in your imagination. Feel worried. Feel the pressure as you get closer and closer to the gate... will you make it?? Ten percent!

meaningMnemonic: The king radical and the king kanji are the same! Hints Hopefully you're a king of radicals... because if you are, this kanji was super easy for you!
readingMnemonic: When you see the king you need to say, " Oh ( おう ) King! Oh King, oh no, oh why are you looking at me like that? Oh King... you aren't going to chop off my head are you? OH NO!" Hints You need to be polite when you talk to the king and add "Oh" to the beginning, otherwise the king will be pretty angry and bad things might happen. We're going to use the 王 kanji for all おう mnemonics from now on. So make sure you always remember to say おう King!

meaningMnemonic: Narwhal s do construction with their left hands (or flippers, I guess). That's because all narwhals are left-handed! Hints Picture a bunch of narwhals constructing an underwater ice village. They're all working away with their left hands.
readingMnemonic: In their left hands, the narwhals all hold saw s ( さ ). That's because the ice for their homes is already there, so they just need to saw away at them to make the shapes they want. Narwhal construction is actually very simple. Hints If you're right-handed, imagine trying to use these left-handed saws. It flips and flops all over until you drop it. But if you're left-handed it feels just right!

meaningMnemonic: The radical middle and the kanji middle are both the same. So if you know one, you know the other. Hints Make sure you're studying your radicals, otherwise you might find yourself in the middle of a kanji-learning problem.
readingMnemonic: To remember the reading for this kanji, we use the word Chewbacca to pull up ちゅう in our memory. If you remember back to the radical 中 , a stick was stuck in the middle of the mouth of something. Let's say it was your mouth, and when you look up to see who did it, there stands Chew bacca. He's even doing his Chewbacca yell. And it isn't a stick in your mouth, it's an arrow from his bowcaster. It just so happens Chewbacca's bowcaster looks just like this kanji too. Go figure. Hints Imagine the fear and shock you'd feel after finding out it was Chewbacca who shot the middle of your mouth (and head). Touch his fur. Look really close at his weapon. Give him a sniff, too. Just so that memory never fades away.

meaningMnemonic: The moon kanji is made up of the moon radical. This kanji is also used to mean month . Hints This should be EZPZ as long as you know the radicals already!
readingMnemonic: The moon really gets ( げつ ) to your guts ( がつ ). Staring at the moon for too long will give you terrible indigestion, so be careful! Hints Use the げつ reading when this kanji means "moon", in words like "moonlight". Use げつ for counting months, and saying things like "last month and "next month", too. Go for がつ in the names of months, like "January". Don't worry too much about memorizing this pattern, though. You'll be getting lots of practice soon!

meaningMnemonic: This is a strange kanji because it doesn't really mean anything at all. In fact, what it does is it repeats the kanji that comes before it. For example: 人々 is actually 人人 . This kanji shows up whenever there's a repeating kanji, because it's often easier to write than writing a more complicated kanji twice. That's why this kanji is the repeater . It repeats what comes before it. To remember that this kanji is the repeater, though, think of a prison with drop s of water dripping over and over in it. Drip drop drip drop. It does that over and over again, driving the prisoners nuts. But it never stops. It just repeats over and over. Hints Since this kanji doesn't really have a meaning as much as it does a function, try to change the way you think about it when you're memorizing it.
readingMnemonic: This symbol doesn't really have a name, but it's sometimes called the のま because it looks like the katakana characters ノ and マ put together. If you know katakana then this will be easy to read. If you don't, think of it this way: Your mom is the repeater . She is trying to force feed you over and over again until you explode (literally). You keep yelling " No ma ( のま )!" but she doesn't stop. She's on a repeating track, never stopping, repeating forever. Hints If you feel like you're so full you're about to burst, and if you imagine your mom doing this to you (how could you, ma?), you should be able to remember the reading of this kanji. That being said, the reading is mostly only useful in the event that you have to identify a 々 — otherwise, you won't see it much.

meaningMnemonic: The rice paddy radical and the rice paddy kanji are the same, making this one super easy to remember, at least meaning-wise. Hints Just know your radicals, and you will know your kanji as well.
readingMnemonic: To remember the reading た , we use the word "taco." You're in the rice field... but when you lean down to examine the rice more closely, you see that it's not rice that's growing, it's a bunch of little ta cos ( た ), blossoming out of the ground. Hints Smell the tacos. Touch the tacos. Taste the tacos. This is definitely a very strange rice field.

meaningMnemonic: Narwhal mouth s are on the right side of their head. In fact, some people didn't think they had mouths at all because they weren't looking from the narwhal's right. Rookie mistake. See how the "mouth" radical is to the right of the "narwhal" radical? That should help you remember that this means right . Hints Imagine looking at a narwhal from the front. No mouth. Now look at it from its right side. Mouth!
readingMnemonic: How did we know to look from its right , though? Because the you ths ( ゆう ) figured it out. Youths think in ways that older people usually don't. That's why they can see the swirls on cereal, hear the music behind noise, and of course, look at things from the right side. Hints Imagine a bunch of youths walking in a group and looking at everything from the right. You remember when you were a youth and you used to look at everything from one side too. Note: All the ゆう readings will use the word "youths" for the reading mnemonic. You can think of these "youths" as a group of younger people who cause a lot of the problems in this world.

meaningMnemonic: Just imagine a beast with a lid for a head and fins for feet, running around looking as insane as possible (really imagine it!). When it runs up to you, it shows you the top of its lid-head. On it is written the numbers 666. Why? Because it's a spawn of the devil, and the number six is the devil's number. Hints Imagine this beast doing various crazy things, the crazier the better (to help you remember). Make sure all these things are associated with the devil and the devil's number ( six ), so you can remember the meaning of this kanji.
readingMnemonic: Whenever we need to remember the reading ろく we just use the word rock . So, think about the devil and the devil's number. What is often associated with those things? Why, rock ( ろく ) and roll is. Imagine the lid-head fin-legged beast suddenly blasting out rock music in the middle of his destructive mayhem. Hints Sing along with the monster, if it helps you to remember the reading of this kanji.

meaningMnemonic: The small radical and the small kanji are exactly the same. Hints Knowing radicals sure is nice, huh?
readingMnemonic: This small kanji would be the perfect gift to give to the Shou gun ( しょう ). The Shougun loves little things, and the little kanji represents all of that. Hints You read that right, shougun is written with a long う sound. Make sure you spell it right from now on!

meaningMnemonic: The radical stand and the kanji stand are the same thing, so now you know them both. Hints If you're keeping up with your radical studies, you're also keeping up with your kanji studies!
readingMnemonic: Think of someone who has to stand up straight for you. These people are pros in hospitality. These are the doormen at the Ritz ( りつ ). Hints Imagine the doormen being extra straight… too straight in their standing. On their uniform is “The Ritz” written in fine lettering, and as you walk past them, they stand up straight and say “Welcome to the Ritz!” Whatever you do, while you’re thinking about it, make sure you think about how they stand up so straight, and associate it with these doormen, who work, specifically, at the Ritz. If you effectively imagine all this, you should be able to remember this on’yomi. Go through it like it’s a movie in your head!

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the radical that look like this are exactly the same. They are both street . Hints As long as you know the radical street, you know the kanji street.
readingMnemonic: So you're walking down this street , and off in the distance you see the silhouette of somebody. A lady. Big, black curly hair and red eyes. It is the street-woman, Mrs. Chou ( ちょう ). Hints Mrs. Chou is a character you'll see a lot throughout WaniKani, anytime the reading is ちょう like this one. A lore will develop around her, so the more vividly you can imagine your Mrs. Chou right now, the easier things will get later. In general, she's a mean, evil woman, so as long as you imagine her within those parameters, you're good. And, when I say she is a "street-woman" in the mnemonic, I don't mean she is homeless. She has a nice, middle-class home that's not outside of her financial means. What I'm saying is she wanders the streets looking for evil things to do. These are HER streets. So whenever you see the street radical, know that Mrs. Chou is probably going to show up!

meaningMnemonic: The sun radical and sun kanji are the same, huzzah! Also, if you want to remember day as well, you can just think about how a day is the time it takes for the sun to cross the sky. Hints The radical for this one is easy too, making the meaning for this kanji super easy as well!
readingMnemonic: There are so many on'yomi for this kanji, but since this kanji is so important and common, you'll end up learning them all eventually whether you want to or not. For now, you're only going to have to learn one of the readings, and that one is にち . The sun is so hot. It focused its rays to take out one man... and that man is Friedrich Nietzsche ( にち ), famous philosopher. He philosophized one too many things about the sun, so the sun decided it was time he paid. Hints This reading will be easier to remember if you know of Friedrich Nietzsche... so do your research and learn about him if you don't. He's a pretty historical dude. Imagine the sun totally pissed off, too. It makes a grunting noise as it builds up a sun beam to blast him off the face of the earth. Also note that there's another reading worth learning as well: じつ . The reading can be remembered by thinking " Gee! Two readings?" Because, seriously, two readings? Too many...

meaningMnemonic: The radical and the meaning of this kanji are almost the same! The radical is sword , but we're learning Japanese, so can you name a Japanese sword ? That's right, the most common is a katana , which happens to be the meaning of this kanji as well. Hints This kanji also looks a lot like the kanji 力 . To avoid getting them confused, remember that this one is missing the little nubbin at the top, because 90% of the power comes from the sword to cut your enemies down (which is why the sword kanji is 90% of the power kanji).
readingMnemonic: So now you have this sweet katana in your hands and you're swinging it around like an idiot. Feel free to make whooshing noises as you swing it around. To become a master katana wielder, you decide to travel to とう きょう (Tokyo). とうきょう has the best sword and katana schools in the world, so it makes sense to travel to とうきょう . Hints Imagine trying to travel to とうきょう with your katana. Airport security is not happy with you trying to take a katana on the plane, so you get a full cavity search. I hope you don't have any other swords hidden anywhere.

meaningMnemonic: On the ground you put barb s at the bottom of a slide . This is your special talent . When you go down the slide, you fly right past the barbs like some kind of daredevil. Any normal kid would land on the barbs and get hurt, but you have this talent. Hints Imagine yourself placing the barbs in front of the slide, thinking about how talented you are. It took years of training to perfect this talent. But it was worth it. Everyone on the playground respects you now.
readingMnemonic: But then people start to say that no human could have so much talent , that you must be a cy borg ( さい ). Are you really a talented cyborg? Hints Cyborgs have brain implants and cool bionic limbs, so they're basically the most talented people around.

meaningMnemonic: This kanji is the same as the radical you learned, so it means thousand . Hints As long as you know the "thousand" radical, you'll know this kanji as well!
readingMnemonic: Remember the thousand people going down the slide on a cross in the radical 千 ? Turns out each one of them was carrying a thousand cen ts ( せん ). Go ahead and try to calculate what a thousand times a thousand cents would come out to. It's quite a lot, actually. Hints Problem is, as they all tumble down the slide the change falls out of their pockets, so there's a thousand times a thousand cents scattered all over on the floor under the slide.

meaningMnemonic: This is another kanji that is the same as the radical. Both tree and tree are the same in looks and meaning. Hints So, how are those radicals doing? Do you know them well?
readingMnemonic: You’re walking through the trees, looking at them. They look ominous. Suddenly, you trip and fall. The trees start to mock ( もく ) you. Even the mocking birds mock you. It’s terrible. It’s painful. You’re being mocked as you pull yourself up off the ground. Hints Feel the shame, feel the irritation. Make yourself want to run away from those dumb trees that are mocking you.

meaningMnemonic: The water radical and the water kanji are the same. Hints So it should already be clear what the kanji means. As clear as… water.
readingMnemonic: When you go swimming, you launch yourself into the water from a tire swi ng ( すい ). It's one of those quintessential summer memories, right? Kids swimming in a lake or pond, flying off a swing and splashing down in the water. In your mind, try to associate water with that swing to remember this reading. Hints Maybe it's a hot rubber tire swing burning your arms (that swing's been hanging in the sun all day), or maybe it's a rope swing grazing your palms. Either way, imagine how that feels as you fly off it, then sense the cold water of the lake or pond suddenly enveloping you. Some of the water even gets into your mouth. Imagine it tastes sweet for some reason. Why? All this sensory stuff tied to the water and swing will help you remember the すい reading later. The more vividly you imagine it the better.

meaningMnemonic: The radical white and the kanji white are the same. Hints Study your radicals hard! Most important thing!
readingMnemonic: The white team was the first to be able to hack ( はく ) the white iPhone. Hints Imagine two teams (black and white ), wearing their team colors, working really hard on hacking the iPhone. It is a huge contest, and people are watching with a lot of tension, to see who will hack the white iPhone first. Feel that tension, and see the colors separating them so vividly. The colors are important, and the excitement of the winner holding up the hack ed iPhone is too.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for writing first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means writing as well. Hints If you can't remember the radical for writing, maybe you could try… writing it down?
readingMnemonic: This kanji has more than one important reading you need to learn! But don't worry, here's a mnemonic to help you: You always put writing on your bun s ( ぶん ) to keep them from getting eaten by the bun mon ster ( もん ). What kind of writing? Usually it's just an X to show the monster these buns are off-limits. (In fact, it kind of looks like the X part in 文 . Hmm…) Hints Imagine writing a big X (or even a big 文 ) on all your buns, then showing them to the bun monster. Watch as he turns and goes at the sight of the writing, all disappointed. Not today, bun monster.

meaningMnemonic: Here we have a head with a lid in it, near the top. Imagine the top of someone's head being closed by a lid. Open that lid up and peer inside... it's full of yen coins, the currency of Japan. Jackpot! And all those yen coins have a nice round shape, naturally. Hints This kanji can mean both "yen" and "round"! It's OK if you can't remember both meanings. But it might help to think about how round the yen coins are inside this person's head, which can also be pretty round…
readingMnemonic: What does the word yen sound like? It sounds like えん . Why? because back in the day, Japanese used to have a "ye" sound, but now it doesn't. Instead, it's an "e" sound, which is why yen = えん ! Hints Picture these round えん in your mind. Maybe look some up online too, just to be safe. See how round those yen ( えん ) are?

meaningMnemonic: 月 in Japanese means "moon" but it also means "month." Why? Probably because the moon takes about a month to get through its cycles. So, what's the fourth moon of the year? Here's a hint, it's the same as the fourth month of the year: April .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. 月 has two on'yomi readings, but since this is a specific month name, it's going to use the がつ reading. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember that: In April , you habitually eat shee p guts ( しがつ ). April is the time for picnics under the cherry blossoms in Japan, and there's nothing you like more than rolling out your picnic blanket and going to town on a big ol' bowl of sheep guts.

sentences.japanese: 四月一日はエイプリルフールです。

sentences.english: Only three more days until April.

sentences.japanese: 四月は、力いっぱいがんばります。
sentences.english: In April, I will try really hard to do my best.

meaningMnemonic: As a single kanji vocab on its own, you know this vocab word has the same meaning as its parent kanji: ball . 玉 can be used for round objects traditionally recognized in Japanese culture, like beads, marbles, pearls, snowballs, and pachinko balls. For balls used in sports, people typically use the katakana word ボール .
readingMnemonic: This word uses the same reading as the one you learned with the kanji: たま .

sentences.english: the knot at the end of a thread

sentences.japanese: ポチは、まるで丸い玉のような犬でした。
sentences.english: Pochi was a dog that looked like a round ball.

sentences.japanese: この玉を力いっぱいキックして下さい。
sentences.english: Please kick this ball with all your strength.

meaningMnemonic: This vocab word is exactly the same as its parent kanji, including its meaning as well: book . It doesn't have those other meanings though, when it's just 本 alone, it's just a book.
readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the single kanji it comes from.

sentences.japanese: この本にはクイズが上手になるためのヒントがかいてある。
sentences.english: This book has hints on how to get better at taking quizzes.

sentences.japanese: うちのオーブンには本がたくさん入ってるんです。
sentences.english: My oven has a lot of books in it.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: You saw a child and gave her your co at ( こ ). The kid looked all cold, so you gave her your coat. Children never want to wear proper warm clothing when they should, then they end up shivering their butts off and needing to wear a parent's oversized coat. Fortunately you were there to give this 子 your coat.

sentences.japanese: そのライオンの子はシンバという。
sentences.english: That lion's child is called Simba.

sentences.japanese: あなたは、わたしのほんとうの子ではないの。
わたしの子、ビヨンセににているとおもわない？
sentences.english: Don’t you think my kid looks similar to Beyoncé?

meaningMnemonic: This vocab word and the kanji that makes it have the same meaning: Circle .
readingMnemonic: The reading you learned for this kanji is the kun'yomi one. Since this vocab word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. Guess what? That means you already know it!

sentences.japanese: ここに丸でチェックして下さい。
sentences.english: Check here with a circle, please.

sentences.japanese: 丸をかくのが上手な人がタイプです。
sentences.english: My type is someone who is good at drawing circles.

sentences.japanese: 人はサプライズでプロポーズされると目が丸になるものなんです。
sentences.english: People get wide-eyed when someone proposes to them as a surprise.

meaningMnemonic: With an い on the end, you can guess that this word is an い -adjective. What is the adjective version of the kanji 丸 ? "Circle" becomes circular , spherical or round . This, compared to another similar word ( 円 ), is more general purpose and can be used with 3D spherical objects as well.
readingMnemonic: This word uses the reading you learned for the kanji 丸 , though you'll need to tack the い onto the end too.

sentences.japanese: このレストランには丸いフルーツしかありません。
sentences.english: This restaurant only serves round-shaped fruit.

sentences.japanese: この玉、ちょっと丸すぎませんか？
sentences.english: Isn't this ball a bit too round?

meaningMnemonic: Ending with an い tells you that this word is an い -adjective. So since you know that the kanji 正 means " correct ," what is the adjective version of that word? Well, it's also correct .
readingMnemonic: This word uses a reading you didn't learn from the kanji. You have to remember the ただ portion in order to read this word, so think about it this way: After you get the answer correct a clown jumps out of nowhere yelling " Ta-da ( ただ )!!!" Imagine it scaring the crap out of you, too.

sentences.japanese: 正しいメールアドレス
ぼくが三日にホテルに入ったというのは正しいです。
sentences.english: It's true that I went into the hotel on the 3rd.

sentences.japanese: 入り口の正しい入り方をおしえてあげましょうか？
sentences.english: Would you like me to show you how to enter an entrance properly?

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. 土 generally refers to dirt or soil or earth .
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. Here's a mnemonic to help you to remember it: You look through the soil. You're trying to find something. As you dig and sift, you come across not one but two chee ses ( つち ). Pull them out of the ground and put them in your mouth. How do the two cheeses taste and compare?

sentences.english: soil used in a rice paddy

sentences.japanese: そのトマト、土がついてるよ。
sentences.english: That tomato has some dirt on it.

sentences.japanese: これはふじ山の土なんだよ。
sentences.english: This is soil from Mt. Fuji.

sentences.japanese: モグラが土に入っていった。
sentences.english: The mole was going into the ground.

meaningMnemonic: This vocab made up of a single kanji shares its meaning with said single kanji. That meaning is dog .
readingMnemonic: Since this is a word made up of a single kanji and nothing else, you can assume that this word will use the kun'yomi reading. The reading you learned for this kanji happens to be the kun'yomi reading as well. So if you know the kanji you know the reading.

sentences.japanese: ぼくのペットは犬です。
この犬は、チワワですか？
うちの犬、ライオンくらいの大きさなんです。
sentences.english: My dog ​​is about the size of a lion.

meaningMnemonic: Eighth day or day eight . No matter how you look at this word, it makes a lot of sense.
readingMnemonic: Words that count days use an exceptional reading. Even though this is a jukugo word, it uses kun'yomi readings for both the kanji. Think about this word this way: Every eighth day you have to buy yo gurt to fuel your ca r ( ようか ). Your car runs on yogurt, but it needs to be refilled every eight days to keep running. It's really inconvenient because it's just ONE day more than a week. And a week just feels better. Oh well.

sentences.japanese: 八日からハワイでバケーションなんです。
sentences.english: I'll be on a vacation in Hawaii from the 8th.

sentences.japanese: とんこつラーメンをつくるのに八日もかかったよ。
sentences.english: It took eight days to make tonkotsu ramen.

sentences.japanese: キムチダイエットは八日でおわった。
sentences.english: The kimchi diet ended after eight days.

meaningMnemonic: The mouth you exit out of is just a doorway (I hope), but an easier way to describe this word or concept is to call it an exit .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. 出口 is an exception to this rule, however, and uses its kun'yomi readings. There's no particular reason why this is, but oftentimes a "body part" word (like mouth) changes a word to use kun'yomi readings instead of on'yomi ones. You already know the kun'yomi reading for 口 ( くち ) from learning the vocab, but to remember the reading for 出 you can think the following: If I exit out this mouth, I'll end up in the ocean (you were swallowed by a whale) and I will surely end up dea d ( で ). Also keep in mind that because of rendaku, くち becomes ぐち .

sentences.japanese: そこは出口ではありません。
このトイレ、出口がないよ。
sentences.english: This bathroom doesn't have an exit.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned for the kanji, meaning you should already know it!

sentences.english: to close one's eyes, to turn a blind eye

sentences.japanese: うちのハスキーは目がブルーです。
そのとき、犬が目に入った。
sentences.english: At that moment, a dog came into sight.

sentences.japanese: 目の下にコンタクトレンズがついてるよ。
sentences.english: There's a contact lens under your eye.

meaningMnemonic: What is an eye ball ? Oh wait, that's easy. It's an eyeball !
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. 目玉 , however, is an exception. Perhaps this is because it includes a body part (the eye) in it, which often makes a word switch to kun'yomi readings. Either way, it doesn't matter too much. Both the readings you learned for the kanji in this word are the kun'yomi, meaning you should know how to read this one. Just make sure you watch out for the rendaku.

sentences.japanese: 目玉をきょろきょろする
サーモンは目玉もおいしいですよ。
sentences.english: Salmon eye balls are tasty too.

sentences.japanese: びっくりして目玉が出るかとおもった。
sentences.english: I was so surprised I thought my eyeballs were going to pop out.

sentences.japanese: セールの目玉はトマトです。
sentences.english: The highlight of the sale is tomatoes.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji 月 means both month and moon (because moon cycles take about a month, presumably). So, what is the number two month? It's not January... it's not March... it's February !
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. 月 has two on'yomi readings, but since this is a specific month name, it's going to use the がつ reading. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember that: February is the month when somebody gives you a knee in the guts ( にがつ ). A complete stranger comes around each February just to knee you right in the guts. Kind of a jerk move, but hey — everyone's got their own way of dealing with the wintertime blues, right?

sentences.japanese: 二月のバレンタインデー
バレンタインデーは二月だよ。
日本の二月は中々さむいですよ。
sentences.english: February in Japan is quite cold.

sentences.japanese: 二月はコートとジャケットのセールがたくさんあります。
sentences.english: There are lots of sales for coats and jackets in February.

meaningMnemonic: Day five or the fifth day . No matter how you look at this word, it makes a lot of sense.
readingMnemonic: Words that count days use an exceptional reading. Even though this is a jukugo word, it uses kun'yomi readings for both the kanji. Think about this word this way: On the fifth day I have to eat ( いつ ) five ca rs ( か ). Now imagine yourself eating five cars. How did you manage to get past the first one? I'm impressed.

sentences.english: a live performance on the fifth

sentences.japanese: ミーティングは五日でもだいじょうぶ？
sentences.english: Is the 5th okay for the meeting?

sentences.japanese: イベントまであと五日。
sentences.english: There are five days left until the event.

sentences.japanese: ああ、あの女の子？デートして五日でフラれたよ。
sentences.english: Oh, that girl? I got dumped five days after we went out on a date.

meaningMnemonic: What happens when you have ten five times? You get fifty !
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. That's the case for this word too, which means you should already know how to read this word.

sentences.japanese: 五十メートルしかウォーキングしなかった。
ママは八日に五十になった。
ポートランドの白人人口は五十パーセントよりも上なんです。
sentences.english: Portland's Caucasian population is higher than 50%.

meaningMnemonic: This vocab is made from a single kanji, which means it shares the same meaning as the parent kanji: fire .
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: What comes off of fire ? Lots and lots of hea t ( ひ ). Feel it coming off the fire, touching and warming your face.

sentences.english: to light a fire, to turn on the stove
to put out fire, to turn off the stove

sentences.japanese: キャンドルに火をつけた。
火がきえるのに五日かかりました。
sentences.english: It took five days to extinguish the fire.

sentences.japanese: ストーブの火をつけるのが上手ですね。
sentences.english: You're good at lighting the stove.

meaningMnemonic: This vocab is made from a single kanji, which means it shares the same meaning as the parent kanji: Five .
readingMnemonic: Since numbers are an exception, this word is read using the on'yomi reading even though it's made from a single kanji all alone. Luckily for you, you learned the reading for this word when you learned the parent kanji.

sentences.japanese: このスマホのスクリーンの大きさは五インチです。
sentences.english: This smartphone screen size is five inches.

sentences.japanese: 五フロアのうちの一フロアはカフェテリアです。
sentences.english: One of the five floors is a cafeteria.

sentences.japanese: 五ゲームおわって、やっとファーストスコアが入った。
sentences.english: After five games, finally there was a first score.

meaningMnemonic: From previous number + つ words, you can probably guess that this word means five things .
readingMnemonic: The reading of this word is the kun'yomi reading of the kanji 五 , meaning you didn't learn it when you learned the parent kanji reading. To remember this word, think of it this way: You have five things . What do you have to do with them? You need to eat ( いつ ) them. Just imagine having five delicious things to eat, sticking each on one finger of your hand, and then eating them one after another. And make sure to count down from five while doing it!

sentences.japanese: バレンタインデーにチョコレートを五つもらった。
sentences.english: I got five chocolates on Valentine's Day.

sentences.japanese: 五つのグループにわかれましょう。
一日で目玉を五つもあつめるなんてムリですよ。
sentences.english: It's impossible to collect five eyeballs in one day.

meaningMnemonic: This vocab word has the same meaning as its parent kanji (single alone kanji usually do that!), meaning it means four .
readingMnemonic: When a vocab is alone like this with no okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) it usually uses its kun'yomi reading. Numbers are an exception, though, and use the on'yomi reading. However, four and seven actually use both. We're going to go with the kun'yomi reading here, and since you haven't learned this reading yet, here's a mnemonic to help you: You have to count to four . But you're tired. One... two... three... * YAWN * ... four. There, you did it. But *yawn* now you can't stop yawning. You're so, so sleepy. Four is too high a number to count without falling asleep. By the way! Both the reading よん and し are pretty common, but because the on'yomi reading し sounds just like the word for "death," it isn't used as much. Generally when you're just counting (for example, "1, 2, 3, 4..."), you will use the reading し . But when you are counting things or people, you'll use よん . There are exceptions to this, but you'll learn them as they come up.

sentences.japanese: わたしのインターナショナルスクールには四クラスありました。
sentences.english: There were four class sections in my international school.

sentences.japanese: この本の四ページには、小さいメッセージがかいてあります。
sentences.english: There's a short message written on the fourth page of this book.

meaningMnemonic: If heaven has given you talent , you must be a genius .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. As long as you know the readings for these kanji, you should be able to read this word just fine.

sentences.japanese: コンピューターの天才
マーケティングの天才
いつか天才テニスプレイヤーとよばれたいです。
sentences.english: I want to be called a genius tennis-player someday.

sentences.japanese: そのゴリラは、まぎれもなく天才だ。
sentences.english: That gorilla is definitely a genius.

meaningMnemonic: A woman child is just a girl ! 女子 is a relatively formal word commonly used in contexts where classification or categorization by gender is used, such as in sports or school settings.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: そっちは女子トイレですよ。
sentences.english: The ladies' room is over there.

sentences.japanese: 女子プロレスのチケットをプレゼントした。
sentences.english: I gave a women's professional wrestling ticket as a present.

sentences.japanese: 女子バレーボールのチームキャプテンでした。
sentences.english: I was the captain of the women's volleyball team.

meaningMnemonic: A woman child is a girl . This word has two kanji with hiragana stuck in the middle. That hiragana is the particle の . This time, it just means the noun before の is modifying the noun after it. 女の子 is a casual word for young girls, like kids or teenagers. Sometimes it can also refer to adult women, but only to playfully or affectionately highlight their youthful or girlish qualities.
readingMnemonic: Since there's hiragana in here, you can bet that these kanji will use the kun'yomi readings. You already know the kun'yomi reading for 女 . You might even remember the one for 子 , but here's a mnemonic just in case: When you need to remember the kun'yomi reading for 子 , just think about how a child stole your co at ( こ ). You gave it to her because she looked cold, but then she ran off down the street and left you shouting, "Coat! Coat! That 子 has my coat!"

sentences.english: a girl who works part-time at one's workplace

sentences.japanese: 女の子のキャラクター
白のドレスの女の子がレイチェルです。
sentences.english: The girl in the white dress is Rachel.

sentences.japanese: この女の子は五才の天才プログラマーだ。
sentences.english: This girl is a five-year-old genius programmer.

sentences.japanese: わたしは女の子じゃない。一人の大人の女。わかった？
sentences.english: I'm not a girl. I'm an adult woman. Got it?

meaningMnemonic: Think of someone holding out their hand. This is average. Things rated below the hand are things you're bad at. Things rated above the hand are things you're good at .
readingMnemonic: Both of these kanji use on'yomi readings, though 手 uses an on'yomi reading you didn't learn with the kanji. It's a rare reading, so it wasn't included (and we just have to deal with exceptions like this as we go along). To remember the reading for this word, here's a mnemonic: What are you good at? You're really good at taking Joe ( じょう ) to the zoo ( ず ). No one else can take Joe to the zoo—he gets mad and throws them into the animal enclosures. But you? Joe trusts you.

sentences.japanese: 上手なコミュニケーション

sentences.english: to be able to do something well

sentences.japanese: コミュニケーション上手
ジェニーさん、スキーが上手ですね。
キアヌ・リーブスのモノマネが上手な人、いませんか？
sentences.english: Is there anyone here who can do a good Keanu Reeves impression?

sentences.japanese: 「はじめまして。」「はじめまして。にほんご上手ですね！」
sentences.english: "Nice to meet you." "Nice to meet you. Your Japanese is good!"

meaningMnemonic: From Ohio ( おはよう ), you shout good morning . Why Ohio? Because that's where you woke up this morning. Imagine yourself waking up in Ohio, and wishing everyone "good morning" at the top of your lungs. おはよう is a casual way to say "good morning." It can also be written in kanji, but hiragana is much more common.

sentences.japanese: マイクに「おはよう」とメールをした。
うーっ、ねむいー、おはよう。

meaningMnemonic: The kanji means hand , and the word means hand too! It can also be used to refer to your whole arm .
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. Since this is a body part, the kun'yomi reading usually takes priority. That means you learned the kun'yomi reading already when you learned the kanji.

sentences.english: to pick up in one's hand
to be available, to obtain something

sentences.japanese: 王は手を上げて「おはよう！」といった。
sentences.english: The king raised his hand and said, "Good morning!"

sentences.japanese: パパの手はモジャモジャだ。

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are… almost the same. The kanji means heaven , but this word is more about the heavens . You know, the great heavens that stretch out high above us? 天 can sometimes refer to religious kinds of heaven (that place we all want to end up someday), but more often it's about the sky and what lies beyond it, so you might also call it the firmament .
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it would normally use the kun'yomi reading. The kanji that makes this word only has one important reading, though, and that happens to be the on'yomi. Since you learned the on'yomi reading for this kanji, you've already learned the reading for this word.

meaningMnemonic: The 々 symbol just repeats the kanji that comes before it. In other words, 中々 is the same as 中中 . Easy! So with 中々 , you have middle x2. When something is more middle than middle itself, it's rather , fairly , or quite something. Why? I guess because those are all good middle-level intensifiers. 中々 can be used in positive or negative ways. In a positive way, it usually means something is better than expected, like 中々おいしい (quite delicious). But it's really versatile and could also mean "a little," "very," or "completely" depending on the situation. It might even sound condescending, so be careful how you use it! In a negative sense, you can use it when something is more difficult than expected, like in 中々できない (can't be done easily).
readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is the kun'yomi reading, since it's like putting two single kanji together rather than a true jukugo word. To learn the kun'yomi reading, take a look at this mnemonic: From the middle of the middle comes a sound. It is a knocking sound. Knock. Knock. Knock. You open up the walls around this thing. Then you open up the second set of walls (middle of the middle). Inside is an old man, who identifies himself as "the knocker." You go inside of him and find another knocker as well. That's why it's a knocker knocker ( なかなか ).

On the sixth day of your roadtrip, you've finally arrived at your destination. You get out of your car and tell it, " Muy ( むい ) bien car ( か ), muy bien!".

meaningMnemonic: This kanji has hiragana attached and ends with an い sound. That means it's probably an adjective (and it is!). readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember the ちい portion: When you think of the word small , try to think of this chee se ea tery ( ちい ). meaningMnemonic: Tenth day or day ten . No matter how you look at this word, it makes a lot of sense.
readingMnemonic: Words that count days use an exceptional reading. Even though this is a jukugo word, it actually uses kun’yomi readings. Think about this word this way: This marks the tenth day since this talker ( とおか ) began talking non-stop. Talkers love talking, but this one is getting quite unbearable… Ten days of talking, can you believe it? Note that とお , generally pronounced "toh" with a long "o" sound, is not a common spelling, and you’ll only see it with a handful of kanji and vocabulary, like in this case. I mean, how often do you encounter a talker who can go on non-stop for ten days? That's pretty rare, right?

meaningMnemonic: This word means to climb . You can tell this word is a verb because it ends with an う sound ( る , in this case). Its meaning is similar to the meaning of the 上 kanji, which is "above." So this word is all about moving "above" something (in other words, climbing!)
readingMnemonic: 上る consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, so it will use the kun'yomi reading of the kanji. If you're not a boy, think about how weird it is that he called you a boy. If you are a grown man, think how you wish he called you "dude" or something, not "boy." If you're a boy, well... think about how appropriate it is that he said "no boy."

meaningMnemonic: Think of someone holding out their hand at shoulder level. Anything above that equals "skillful." Everything below that hand equals unskillful . That's why "below hand" means unskilled or bad at !

meaningMnemonic: Although this word consists of one kanji that is all alone, it doesn't share its meaning with the parent kanji. But the meanings are similar in a way. This word means years old or age . With more years comes more talent , right? That's why this word means "years old" and not "talent," like the parent kanji. You can stick this word onto numbers to say how old someone is! Special note for all of you advanced learners out there. When discussing age, 〜歳 is the original and correct kanji to use. Because 〜才 is easier to write and has the same reading, it became mainstream. You'll see it used in writing today, especially in elementary schools. In formal writing though, you'll always want to use 〜歳 , which you'll learn later on.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned for the kanji, meaning you should already know it! Don't try to type the 〜 part though.
